query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In as‐cast, Co-free FeNiCrMn, dynamic mechanical behavior is governed by a competition between thermally activated dislocation glide and the formation of localized adiabatic shear bands. At high strain rates and low temperatures, limited thermal activation increases dislocation drag and pile‐up, triggering shear band initiation that enhances yield strength while reducing ductility. At higher temperatures, enhanced thermal recovery suppresses shear band formation, resulting in more homogeneous deformation and a balanced strength–ductility response.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified (as‐cast) Co‐free FeNiCrMn with inherent microstructural heterogeneities.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to dynamic mechanical tests (e.g., dynamic compression) over a controlled range of strain rates and temperatures.
generation.conditions: Strain rates from quasi‐static (~10^−3 s^−1) to high (∼10^3 s^−1) and temperatures ranging from cryogenic (~77 K) to elevated (∼300–500 K) conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized adiabatic shear bands and variations in dislocation density within the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Under high strain rate and/or low-temperature conditions, dislocation motion is hindered by reduced thermal activation, promoting dislocation pile-ups and triggering localized adiabatic shear band formation. These shear bands concentrate plastic deformation, thus enhancing yield strength but reducing ductility. Conversely, at elevated temperatures, increased dislocation mobility and dynamic recovery lead to more uniform deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: At high strain rates and low temperatures, the material will display increased yield strength and reduced ductility, accompanied by the appearance of adiabatic shear bands and elevated local dislocation densities. At higher temperatures, deformation will be more homogeneous with lower yield strength and improved ductility.
generation.baseline: Quasi-static loading at room temperature where the deformation is relatively homogeneous, with lower yield strength and higher ductility.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to as-cast, Co-free FeNiCrMn and may not hold for samples that have undergone significant post-solidification processing or annealing which alter their microstructural features.
generation.uncertainty: Exact strain rate and temperature thresholds for the transition to shear band–dominated deformation are not precisely determined and may vary with slight compositional or microstructural differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct controlled dynamic compression tests on as-cast FeNiCrMn specimens using a split-Hopkinson pressure bar, across a matrix of temperatures (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 500 K) and strain rates (from 10^-3 s^-1 to 10^3 s^-1). Combine the tests with high-speed imaging, digital image correlation, and post-mortem SEM/TEM analyses to assess the presence, density, and morphology of adiabatic shear bands and measure dislocation density.
measurements: Stress–strain responses (yield strength, ultimate strength, ductility)
Local deformation patterns using high-speed imaging and digital image correlation
Microstructural characterization (shear band formation, dislocation density) via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under high strain rate and low temperature conditions, there is no significant increase in yield strength or decrease in ductility relative to quasi-static room temperature tests, or if high-speed imaging and microstructural analyses do not reveal the initiation or presence of localized adiabatic shear bands, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new alloys that contain five or more elements in roughly-equal proportion. We present new experiments and theory on the deformation behavior of HEAs under slow stretching (straining), and observe differences, compared to conventional alloys with fewer elements. For a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates, HEAs deform in a jerky way, with sudden slips that make it difficult to precisely control the deformation. An analytic model explains these slips as avalanches of slipping weak spots and predicts the observed slip statistics, stress-strain curves, and their dependence on temperature, strain-rate, and material composition. The ratio of the weak spots’ healing rate to the strain-rate is the main tuning parameter, reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier effect and time-temperature superposition in polymers. Our model predictions agree with the experimental results. The proposed widely-applicable deformation mechanism is useful for deformation control and alloy design.
